You are reverse-engineering a Python program by BLACK-BOX probing. You may NOT read Python library source.

The program is at /workspace/dataset/test6_executable and its Python source is:

    import argparse
    from furl import furl
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--c', type=str, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    f = furl(args.a)
    print(f.scheme)
    print(f.host)
    print(f.path)
    print(f.query.add({args.b: args.c}))
    print(f.url)

Invoke it as:  /workspace/dataset/test6_executable --a "<URL>" --b "<KEY>" --c "<VAL>"
All three args are REQUIRED. It prints exactly 5 lines:
  line1 = f.scheme      (Python None prints as "None"; empty string prints as "")
  line2 = f.host
  line3 = f.path
  line4 = str(f.query) AFTER add({b: c})
  line5 = f.url AFTER that mutation

PROBING TECHNIQUE:
- Use a bash helper so output is unambiguous. Example:
    p(){ echo "IN=[$1] b=[$2] c=[$3]"; /workspace/dataset/test6_executable --a "$1" --b "$2" --c "$3" 2>&1 | cat -A; echo "rc=$?"; }
  cat -A makes trailing spaces / CR / non-ascii visible ($ = end of line, M- sequences = high bytes).
- Use single quotes in bash to avoid shell mangling.
- To distinguish "empty string" from "None" on a line: cat -A shows "$" for empty and "None$" for None.
- Note lines 4 and 5 reflect the MUTATION (the added b=c pair). To see the *original* query you must
  reason by subtracting the appended pair, or use a b/c pair you can recognize (e.g. b=Z c=Z).
- Some inputs may make the program CRASH (traceback) or exit nonzero. Record those exactly:
  the exception type and message matter, but for our port we mainly need to know WHICH inputs crash.
- Run MANY probes (30+). Be systematic: vary one thing at a time. Confirm every rule with at least
  two independent examples, and actively try to FALSIFY each rule you form.

OUTPUT CONTRACT: return findings as structured data. Rules must be precise enough that another engineer
can implement them in JavaScript WITHOUT running the executable. Always attach the literal probe
transcripts (exact argv you passed, exact 5 output lines) that justify each rule.


DIMENSION: QUERY PARSING (splitting the incoming query string into pairs).
Focus on how the ORIGINAL query string in --a is parsed and then re-serialized on line4/line5.
Probe --b Z --c Z consistently so you can subtract the appended "&Z=Z".
Test query strings: "a=1&b=2", "a=1&a=2" (duplicate keys preserved and ordered?),
"a" (key with no equals), "a=" (empty value), "=1" (empty key), "=" , "&" , "&&a=1&&",
"a=1&&b=2", "a==1", "a=1=2", ";" as a separator ("a=1;b=2" — is semicolon a separator?),
empty query ("http://h/p?"), no query at all, "a=1&" trailing ampersand,
plus handling: "a=b+c" (is plus decoded to space and re-encoded?), "a=b%20c", "a=b%2Bc",
"%26" and "%3D" inside keys and values, a key or value containing a raw space,
a query containing "#", a query appearing before a fragment "?a=1#f",
and a URL with "?" inside the fragment "http://h/p#frag?x=1" (does furl treat that as fragment query?).
Report: the exact separator rules, whether ordering is preserved, whether empty pairs are dropped,
and how a bare key (no equals) is re-serialized.

rules.rule: Query extraction: the fragment is cut off first at the FIRST '#', then the query is everything after the FIRST '?' in the remainder. A '?' that appears after a '#' belongs to the fragment and is never parsed as a query. A second '?' inside the query is an ordinary literal query character (it percent-encodes to %3F).
rules.evidence:
argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1#f' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&Z=Z#f
argv: --a 'http://h/p#frag?x=1' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | Z=Z | http://h/p?Z=Z#frag?x=1   (query is EMPTY; the '?x=1' stayed in the fragment)
argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1#f?x=2' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&Z=Z#f?x=2
argv: --a 'http://h/p??a=1' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | %3Fa=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?%3Fa=1&Z=Z   (query string is '?a=1', key='?a')
argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1?b=2' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a=1%3Fb%3D2&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1%3Fb%3D2&Z=Z

rules.rule: Pre-processing: every ASCII TAB (0x09), LF (0x0A) and CR (0x0D) byte is REMOVED from the URL string before parsing (they vanish entirely, they are not encoded). No other control character is removed — 0x01, 0x0B (VT) and 0x0C (FF) survive and are percent-encoded. A raw space also survives (and becomes '+').

argv: --a $'http://h/p?a=x\ty&b=2' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a=xy&b=2&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=xy&b=2&Z=Z

argv: --a $'http://h/p?a=x\ry' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a=xy&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=xy&Z=Z
argv: --a $'http://h/p?a=x\vy' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a=x%0By&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=x%0By&Z=Z

argv: --a $'http://h/p?a=x\x01y' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a=x%01y&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=x%01y&Z=Z
NOTE: a %09 / %0A written as a percent-escape is NOT removed: --a 'http://h/p?a=%09' -> line4 'a=%09&Z=Z'.

rules.rule: If the extracted query string is the empty string (URL has no '?' at all, or ends in '?', or has '?#frag'), the pair list is EMPTY (zero pairs) — it is NOT one empty pair.
rules.evidence:

argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | Z=Z | http://h/p?Z=Z
argv: --a 'http://h/p?#f' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | Z=Z | http://h/p?Z=Z#f

rules.rule: Separator: the ONLY pair separator is '&'. Semicolon ';' is NOT a separator — it is an ordinary character that ends up inside a key or value and is re-encoded as %3B. A percent-encoded '%26' is likewise not a separator.
rules.evidence:
argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1;b=2' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a=1%3Bb%3D2&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1%3Bb%3D2&Z=Z   (ONE pair: key='a', value='1;b=2')
argv: --a 'http://h/p?a;b=1' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a%3Bb=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?a%3Bb=1&Z=Z
argv: --a 'http://h/p?;a=1' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | %3Ba=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?%3Ba=1&Z=Z
argv: --a 'http://h/p?a%26b=1' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a%26b=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?a%26b=1&Z=Z   (ONE pair, key='a&b')

rules.rule: Splitting is a plain str.split('&') with NO dropping of empty parts: a query with N '&' characters yields exactly N+1 pairs, and empty parts become pairs with key='' and value=None which re-serialize as the empty string. Leading, trailing and consecutive '&' are all preserved verbatim across the round trip.
rules.evidence:
argv: --a 'http://h/p?&' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | &&Z=Z | http://h/p?&&Z=Z   (2 empty pairs)
argv: --a 'http://h/p?&&&' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | &&&&Z=Z | http://h/p?&&&&Z=Z   (4 empty pairs)

argv: --a 'http://h/p?&a=1&&b&=2&c=&' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | &a=1&&b&=2&c=&&Z=Z | http://h/p?&a=1&&b&=2&c=&&Z=Z

rules.rule: Within a part, the split is on the FIRST '=' only: key = text before it, value = everything after it (which may itself contain '='). If the part contains no '=' at all, the pair is a BARE KEY: key = whole part, value = None.
rules.evidence:

argv: --a 'http://h/p?a===b' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a=%3D%3Db&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=%3D%3Db&Z=Z

rules.rule: A bare key (value None) re-serializes as just the encoded key with NO trailing '='; a key with an explicitly empty value re-serializes as 'key='. The two are distinguishable and round-trip faithfully. An empty key with an empty value round-trips as '='.
rules.evidence:

argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a=&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=&Z=Z

argv: --a 'http://h/p?=1' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | =1&Z=Z | http://h/p?=1&Z=Z

rules.rule: Order is strictly preserved (insertion order, no sorting, no case folding) and duplicate keys are ALL kept as separate pairs.

rules.rule: Each key and value is fully DECODED at parse time and RE-ENCODED at serialize time (it is not preserved verbatim). Decoding: '+' -> space, and '%XX' -> byte, then the byte string is decoded as UTF-8 with errors='replace'. Consequences: '%41' becomes 'A', '%20' and '+' and a raw space all become a space, '%3d' becomes '=', and any invalid UTF-8 byte sequence becomes U+FFFD.

uncertainties: The empty-key '=' quirk (rule 12) is reproduced consistently across 8+ probes, but the exact internal cause is unknown. I verified it is a SERIALIZER behavior (it fires for a pair supplied via --b '' --c 'a=b', not just for parsed input) and that it applies to ALL '=' in the value, not only the first. I could NOT construct a case where a bare key (value None) is empty AND contains '=' to see whether the same exemption applies there, because any '=' in a part forces a key/value split and add() never produces a None value.
Whether the '=' exemption depends on key === '' exactly, or on 'the encoded key is empty'. These are indistinguishable with the available inputs since no non-empty string encodes to the empty string.

Leading whitespace on the whole --a argument has a side effect outside this dimension: '  http://h/p?a=1  ' returned scheme=None, host=None, path=/p and query 'a=1++' — the leading '  http://h' portion disappeared from f.url entirely. I did not chase this down; it belongs to the URL/authority-parsing dimension, but it means a JS port must not assume the query offset is computed on the raw string in that case. Trailing spaces DO become '+' in the last value.

I did not test whether furl's query delimiter can be affected by an extremely long query, by NUL bytes in the actual argv (shell cannot pass them), or by surrogate/astral characters beyond the café / 中 cases tested.

No input produced a crash or non-zero exit in ~90 probes, so I have no evidence about which inputs (if any) raise. I cannot rule out crashes for inputs I did not try (e.g. IDN hosts, extremely long inputs).
